definition: A system that perceives its environment through sensors and acts on that environment through actuators.
wrongs: A database table that stores records but never senses or acts.
A sorting routine that orders an array and then stops.
A network cable that only carries bits between two sockets.
why: The agent idea pairs ongoing perception with actions chosen in response to that perception.
example: A thermostat reads the room temperature and switches the heater on or off.
scenario: A robot reads a camera and turns its wheels in response. Which AI idea describes that pairing of sensing and acting?
scenarioWhy: An intelligent agent is defined by perceiving an environment and acting on it.

definition: Choosing actions expected to maximize a performance measure, given the percepts and built-in knowledge so far.
wrongs: Choosing actions that always take the longest possible path.
Ignoring the performance measure and acting at random forever.
Copying the previous percept into a file without acting.
why: A rational agent is judged by expected success on its performance measure, not by having perfect foresight.
example: A vacuum agent that has seen dirt in this square chooses to clean it because that raises its cleanliness score.
scenario: A vacuum scores points for clean squares and can see dirt in the current square. Which action is rational?
scenarioWrongs: Leave the dirt and spin in place
scenarioWhy: Cleaning the observed dirt is the action expected to improve the cleanliness score.

definition: The input an agent's sensors provide at one moment about the environment.
wrongs: The motor command the agent sends to an actuator.
The long-term performance score printed at the end of a run.
The source code of the agent program.
why: Percepts are the agent's sensory inputs, and a percept sequence is the history of those inputs.
example: A camera frame showing a red light is the current percept of a driving agent.
scenario: A driving program receives one camera frame of a red light before it chooses an action. What is that frame?
scenarioWhy: A percept is the sensory input available to the agent at that moment.

definition: A component through which an agent changes the environment, such as a motor or a display.
wrongs: A sensor that only measures the environment.
A heuristic number stored in a search node.
A label attached to a training example.
why: Actuators carry out actions, while sensors supply percepts.
example: The wheels of a robot vacuum are actuators because they move the robot to a new square.
scenario: A robot vacuum needs a part that moves it into the next square rather than a part that only senses dirt. Which part is that?
scenarioWhy: An actuator is the component that carries out an action on the environment.

definition: A task description listing performance measure, environment, actuators, and sensors.
wrongs: A search formula that adds path cost to a heuristic.
A logic rule with only conditions and a conclusion.
A training set split into labeled and unlabeled rows.
why: PEAS names the four parts needed to specify a rational-agent task before choosing a design.
example: For a chess program, PEAS lists win rate, the board and opponent, the move output, and the board sensor.
scenario: Designers list success criteria, the world, the outputs, and the inputs of a taxi agent before building it. Which description is that?
scenarioWhy: PEAS is the four-part task description: performance, environment, actuators, and sensors.

definition: An environment in which the agent's sensors show the complete state relevant to its choice at each moment.
wrongs: An environment in which parts of the relevant state stay hidden from the sensors.
An environment whose next state is random even when the full state is known.
An environment that changes while the agent is still deciding.
why: Full observability means the percept contains what the agent needs to know about the current state.
example: In a standard chess program, the current board position is fully visible before each move.
scenario: A puzzle agent can see every tile's location before it chooses a move. How is that environment classified?
scenarioWrongs: Stochastic because some tiles are hidden
Dynamic only because the tiles are visible
scenarioWhy: The sensors reveal the whole relevant state, so the environment is fully observable.

definition: An environment whose next state is fixed by the current state and the action, with no random outcome.
wrongs: An environment in which the same action can lead to several possible next states by chance.
An environment that hides part of the state from the agent.
An environment that contains several independent agents.
why: Determinism means the transition is certain once the state and action are known.
example: On an empty 8-puzzle board model, sliding a tile always produces the same next arrangement.
scenario: Sliding one tile on an 8-puzzle model always yields the same next board. Which environment property is that?
scenarioWhy: The next state is completely determined by the current board and the slide.

definition: An environment divided into independent episodes, where the action in one does not affect later episodes.
wrongs: An environment in which each action changes the state faced by every later decision.
An environment whose map is a single long path with no separate episodes.
An environment that is fully observable and therefore must be sequential.
why: In an episodic setting, the agent can choose for the current episode without planning across future episodes.
example: A factory camera classifies each part on the belt separately, and one classification does not change the next part.
scenario: A vision system labels each item on a belt, and one label does not change the next item. Which task type is that?
scenarioWrongs: Dynamic solely because labels are independent
scenarioWhy: Each classification is its own episode and does not affect the next item's state.

definition: An environment that does not change while the agent is deliberating.
wrongs: An environment that keeps changing during the time the agent spends choosing.
An environment whose next state is random.
An environment that hides its state from the sensors.
why: If nothing else changes during deliberation, the state the agent analyzed is still the state it acts on.
example: A crossword puzzle stays the same while a program spends a minute choosing the next letter.
scenario: A crossword grid does not change during the minute a program spends choosing a letter. Which property is that?
scenarioWhy: The environment is static because it does not change while the agent deliberates.

definition: An agent that chooses its action from the current percept alone, using condition-action rules.
wrongs: An agent that keeps an internal model of how the world evolves.
An agent that compares future paths against an explicit goal.
An agent that selects the action with the highest expected utility.
why: A simple reflex agent does not store a model of unseen state; the current percept selects the rule.
example: A vacuum rule says that if the current square is dirty, the action is to suck, with no map of other rooms.
scenario: A vacuum has only the rule: if this square is dirty, suck. It keeps no map and no goal test. Which agent type is that?
scenarioWrongs: A model-based agent that tracks unseen rooms
scenarioWhy: The action comes directly from the current percept through a condition-action rule.

definition: An agent that chooses actions by considering which future states would reach a declared goal.
wrongs: An agent that reacts only to the current percept and never considers the future.
An agent that maximizes a numeric happiness score among several acceptable goals.
An agent that learns weights from labeled examples and has no explicit goal test.
why: Goal-based behavior asks whether a sequence of actions leads to a state that passes the goal test.
example: A route finder chooses turns by searching for a path that reaches the stated destination intersection.
scenario: A navigator searches future turns until the state matches a declared destination. Which agent type is that?
scenarioWrongs: An agent with no goal test that only mimics labels
scenarioWhy: The navigator chooses actions by testing whether future states reach the goal.

definition: An agent that chooses the action with the highest expected utility when several outcomes are possible.
wrongs: An agent that stops at the first state passing a yes-or-no goal test, with no preference among goals.
An agent that applies a reflex rule to the current percept only.
An agent that stores facts but never selects an action.
why: Utility ranks outcomes, so the agent can prefer a safer or better success instead of any goal state.
example: A delivery robot prefers a slightly longer road with a higher chance of arriving undamaged over a risky shortcut.
scenario: Two routes both reach the customer, but one is safer. The robot prefers the higher expected score. Which agent type is that?
scenarioWrongs: A pure goal agent with no ranking among successes
A knowledge base with no actions
scenarioWhy: The robot ranks outcomes by expected utility rather than treating every successful route as equal.

definition: The set of all states that a search problem can reach from the initial state by legal actions.
wrongs: Only the single goal state, excluding every other configuration.
The list of training labels for a classifier.
The set of English words in an expert-system explanation.
why: Search explores the state space by applying actions that move from one state to a neighboring state.
example: For the 8-puzzle, the state space is every reachable arrangement of the eight tiles and the blank.
scenario: An 8-puzzle solver must consider every reachable arrangement of tiles, not only the solved board. What is that set called?
scenarioWhy: The state space contains all configurations the legal moves can reach.

definition: A record in a search tree that stores a state, a parent link, the action used, and the path cost.
wrongs: The physical city on a map, with no parent pointer or path cost.
A labeled training example in a data table.
A rule in an expert-system knowledge base.
why: The node is the search bookkeeping around a state, which is why two nodes can contain the same state.
example: A route search stores a node for each partial path, including the city reached and the cost so far.
scenario: A router search must remember a city, how it was reached, and the cost so far. What record holds those fields?
scenarioWrongs: The city itself with no path data
scenarioWhy: A search node stores the state together with its parent, action, and path cost.

definition: The total cost of the actions along the path from the initial state to a given node.
wrongs: A heuristic estimate of the remaining cost from the node to the goal.
The number of labels in a training set.
The depth limit chosen before a search begins.
why: Path cost, often written g(n), adds the step costs already taken and does not estimate the future.
example: A driving search adds 12 km and then 7 km, so the path cost of that node is 19 km.
scenario: A node was reached by traveling 12 km and then 7 km. Which quantity is 19 km?
scenarioWrongs: The heuristic estimate to the goal
scenarioWhy: Path cost is the sum of the step costs already used to reach the node.

definition: An uninformed search that expands the shallowest unexpanded node before any deeper node.
wrongs: A search that always expands the deepest unexpanded node first.
A search that expands the node with the lowest path cost plus heuristic.
A local search that only moves to a better neighbor.
why: Using a queue makes breadth-first search explore level by level from the start.
example: On an unweighted subway map, breadth-first search finds a route with the fewest stops.
scenario: Every step has equal cost, and the solver must find a route with the fewest steps. Which uninformed search fits?
scenarioWhy: Breadth-first search expands level by level, so the first goal it reaches has the fewest steps.

definition: An uninformed search that expands the deepest unexpanded node before its shallower siblings.
wrongs: A search that expands every node at the current depth before going deeper.
A search that expands the lowest path-cost node next.
A search that uses a heuristic to jump toward the goal.
why: A stack, or recursion, sends depth-first search down one branch before it backtracks.
example: A maze program follows one corridor as far as it can, then backtracks to the last choice.
scenario: A maze program should follow one corridor to its end before trying the previous junction. Which search matches?
scenarioWhy: Depth-first search goes deep along one branch and backtracks only when that branch is exhausted.

definition: A search that repeats depth-limited depth-first search, increasing the depth limit by one each time.
wrongs: A single breadth-first search that stores every node of the current level.
A best-first search guided only by a heuristic.
A local search that restarts from a random state.
why: The repeated depth limits give the short-solution guarantee of breadth-first search with less memory.
example: A puzzle solver tries depth 1, then depth 2, then depth 3, using depth-first search inside each limit.
scenario: A solver wants the shortest unweighted solution but cannot store a whole breadth-first frontier. Which search fits?
scenarioWrongs: Plain depth-first search with no depth limit
scenarioWhy: Iterative deepening finds the shallowest solution by increasing a depth-first limit one step at a time.

definition: An uninformed search that expands the node with the smallest path cost from the start.
wrongs: A search that expands the shallowest node even when step costs differ.
A search that expands the node that looks closest to the goal.
A search that expands the deepest node first.
why: Expanding the lowest g(n) first yields an optimal path when every step cost is nonnegative.
example: On a map with different road lengths, uniform-cost search expands the partial route whose kilometers so far are smallest.
scenario: Road segments have unequal lengths, all positive, and no heuristic is available. Which search finds a cheapest route?
scenarioWhy: Uniform-cost search expands the lowest path cost first and is optimal for nonnegative step costs.

definition: A search that uses only the problem definition and no extra estimate of distance to the goal.
wrongs: A search that ranks nodes with a heuristic estimate of remaining cost.
A learning method that fits labeled examples.
A logic method that chains rules from known facts.
why: Uninformed algorithms such as breadth-first and uniform-cost search do not receive a heuristic.
example: Breadth-first search explores a maze using only the legal moves, with no estimate of distance to the exit.
scenario: A maze solver may use the start, the moves, and the goal test, but it has no distance estimate. Which search family is that?
scenarioWhy: Uninformed search has the problem definition only and no heuristic guidance.

definition: A problem-specific estimate of the cheapest cost from a state to a goal, used to guide search.
wrongs: The exact path cost already spent from the start to the node.
A label that states the correct class of a training example.
A condition-action rule in a reflex agent.
why: A heuristic, h(n), estimates remaining cost and is extra information beyond the bare problem definition.
example: A map search uses straight-line distance to the destination as an estimate of remaining road distance.
scenario: A map program estimates remaining distance by the straight line to the goal, which may be shorter than the roads. What is that estimate?
scenarioWrongs: The exact path cost already traveled
scenarioWhy: Straight-line distance is a heuristic estimate of the remaining cost, not the cost already paid.

definition: A best-first search that expands the node with the smallest f(n), where f(n) adds path cost and a heuristic.
wrongs: A search that expands the shallowest node and ignores both cost and estimates.
A search that follows only the heuristic and ignores cost already spent.
A search that expands the deepest node on a stack.
why: Adding g(n) and h(n) accounts for both the cost already used and the estimated cost remaining.
example: A navigation app expands the junction whose driven kilometers plus straight-line estimate is currently smallest.
scenario: A router should add kilometers already driven to a straight-line estimate and expand the smallest total. Which search is that?
scenarioWhy: A* expands the node with the lowest sum of path cost and heuristic estimate.

definition: An informed search that expands the node whose heuristic estimate to the goal is smallest, ignoring path cost.
wrongs: A search that expands the node with the smallest sum of path cost and heuristic.
A search that expands the lowest path cost and uses no heuristic.
A search that expands nodes level by level.
why: Because it follows only h(n), it can head toward the goal quickly and still miss a cheaper path.
example: A hiker always walks toward the ridge that looks closest to the peak and ignores how far the hike has already been.
scenario: A program always expands the city that appears closest to the destination and ignores distance already traveled. Which search is that?
scenarioWhy: Greedy best-first search ranks nodes by the heuristic alone.

definition: A heuristic that never estimates a cost higher than the true cheapest cost from that state to a goal.
wrongs: A heuristic that sometimes estimates more than the true remaining cost.
A path cost that records distance already traveled.
A random number unrelated to the goal.
why: Admissibility keeps h(n) optimistic, which is what tree-search A* needs in order to stay optimal.
example: Straight-line distance is admissible for road search because a road route cannot be shorter than the straight line.
scenario: A road heuristic never claims a remaining distance longer than the best real route. Which property does it have?
scenarioWrongs: It equals the distance already driven
scenarioWhy: An admissible heuristic never overestimates the true remaining cost.

definition: A heuristic for which the estimate at a node is no greater than the step to a neighbor plus the estimate at that neighbor.
wrongs: A heuristic that only promises never to overestimate, with no triangle condition on each step.
A search that stores every generated state in a closed set.
A cost function that can be negative.
why: Consistency, also called monotonicity, is the condition used to guarantee optimal A* graph search.
example: A grid heuristic of Manhattan distance drops by at most the cost of one legal step when the agent takes that step.
scenario: For every move, a grid heuristic falls by no more than that move's cost. Which stronger heuristic property is that?
scenarioWrongs: Mere storage in a closed set
scenarioWhy: Consistency says the heuristic cannot drop by more than the cost of the step just taken.

definition: The guarantee that a search algorithm will find a solution whenever at least one solution exists.
wrongs: The guarantee that the first solution found is always a cheapest solution.
The guarantee that memory use stays constant as the map grows.
The guarantee that a heuristic never overestimates.
why: Completeness is about eventually finding some solution, which is separate from finding a lowest-cost one.
example: Breadth-first search on a finite unweighted maze is complete because it will reach an exit if any path exists.
scenario: On a finite maze, a search is sure to reach an exit if any path exists, even if that path is not cheapest. Which guarantee is that?
scenarioWhy: Completeness promises that an existing solution will be found, not that it is the cheapest.

definition: The guarantee that a search algorithm returns a lowest-cost solution among all possible solutions.
wrongs: The guarantee only that some solution will be found, with no claim about cost.
The guarantee that the search uses a stack.
The guarantee that every heuristic is consistent.
why: Optimality concerns the cost of the solution returned, not merely whether a solution appears.
example: Uniform-cost search on a map with positive road lengths returns a route whose total length is minimal.
scenario: With positive segment costs and no heuristic, a search returns a route of truly minimal length. Which guarantee is that?
scenarioWhy: Optimality means the solution that is returned has the lowest path cost.

definition: The number of legal successor actions, or child nodes, generated from a typical state.
wrongs: The cost of the cheapest path from the start.
The depth of the shallowest goal.
The number of training examples.
why: The branching factor controls how fast the number of nodes grows with depth.
example: If every room in a dungeon has three doors, the search tree's branching factor is about three.
scenario: Each puzzle state has four legal moves. Which quantity describes how many children a typical node has?
scenarioWrongs: The size of the training set
scenarioWhy: The branching factor is the number of successors expanded from a typical state.

definition: A search that grows one tree forward from the start and another backward from the goal until they meet.
wrongs: A search that expands only from the start until it happens to reach the goal.
A local search that climbs from one random state.
A depth-first search that never records the goal until the end.
why: Meeting in the middle can explore far fewer nodes than searching the full depth from one side alone.
example: A subway planner searches outward from the home station and backward from the campus station until a common station appears.
scenario: A planner searches from home and from campus at the same time until the two frontiers share a station. Which search is that?
scenarioWhy: Bidirectional search runs from the start and the goal until the two searches meet.

definition: A model that is too simple to capture the regular pattern in the training examples.
wrongs: A model that memorizes training noise and then fails on new examples.
A search that expands nodes in depth order.
A heuristic that never overestimates remaining cost.
why: Underfitting shows high error even on the training data because the hypothesis cannot represent the real pattern.
example: A straight line is fitted to points that clearly form a curve, so both training and new points stay far from the line.
scenario: Points form a curve, but the chosen model is a straight line and misses badly even on the training points. What problem is that?
scenarioWhy: Underfitting is a model too simple to represent the pattern, so training error stays high.

definition: A local search that repeatedly moves to a neighboring state with a better value until no neighbor is better.
wrongs: A systematic search that keeps a frontier of all shallow partial paths.
A search that restarts from the initial state with a deeper limit.
A logical proof that chains every rule in a knowledge base.
why: Hill climbing looks only at local neighbors, so it never keeps a frontier of distant alternative paths.
example: A timetable program swaps two classes whenever the swap reduces conflicts and stops when no swap helps.
scenario: A scheduler keeps a swap of two classes only when the swap reduces conflicts, then stops when none helps. Which method is that?
scenarioWhy: Hill climbing accepts a better neighbor and stops when every neighbor is worse.

definition: A state whose neighbors are all worse, even though a better state exists somewhere else.
wrongs: A state that has a better neighbor one move away.
The best state in the entire state space.
The initial state before any move is tried.
why: Hill climbing stops at a local maximum because every immediate move looks worse.
example: A route around a small hill is shorter than every adjacent tweak, yet a completely different road is shorter still.
scenario: Every small change of a schedule adds conflicts, yet a very different schedule has fewer conflicts. What is the current schedule?
scenarioWrongs: A state with a better neighbor
scenarioWhy: A local maximum is worse than some distant state but better than all of its neighbors.

definition: A local search that sometimes accepts a worse neighbor, with that probability decreasing over time.
wrongs: A local search that never accepts a worse neighbor.
A uniformed breadth-first search of the whole space.
A proof procedure that accepts a conclusion only when a rule matches.
why: Early acceptance of worse moves can escape local maxima, and the falling chance lets the search settle.
example: A layout program occasionally keeps a slightly worse placement at the start, then almost never does so near the end.
scenario: A layout search sometimes keeps a worse placement early, then almost never does so later. Which method matches?
scenarioWhy: Simulated annealing allows worse moves with a probability that decreases as the search continues.

definition: An adversarial search that chooses a move by assuming the opponent also plays optimally in a zero-sum game.
wrongs: A one-player search that ignores any opponent.
A learning method that fits labels with no game tree.
A reflex rule that looks only at the current square.
why: The maximizer picks the highest value, and each minimizer node picks the lowest value for the maximizer.
example: A tic-tac-toe program looks to the end and chooses the move that wins even if the opponent answers perfectly.
scenario: A tic-tac-toe program assumes the opponent will answer perfectly and picks the least bad guaranteed result. Which method is that?
scenarioWhy: Minimax selects a move under the assumption of optimal play by the opponent.

definition: A minimax speedup that skips branches that cannot change the decision already available at a higher node.
wrongs: A change that makes minimax choose a different move than full minimax would.
A heuristic that replaces the game rules.
A breadth-first search of a one-player maze.
why: Pruned branches cannot affect the minimax value, so the chosen move stays the same as full minimax.
example: After one chess line is valued at +2, the program skips a later line once it sees the opponent can hold it to 0.
scenario: A game search skips a line once it knows the opponent can force a worse value than a line already found. What speedup is that?
scenarioWrongs: Changing the minimax move on purpose
Replacing the rules with a coin flip
scenarioWhy: Alpha-beta pruning cuts branches that cannot change the minimax decision.

definition: A static score that estimates how favorable a game position is without searching all the way to the end.
wrongs: The exact minimax value of a fully solved terminal position only.
The path cost from the start in a one-player route problem.
The label of a supervised training example.
why: When the game tree is too deep, the evaluation function scores a cutoff position for minimax.
example: A chess program scores material and king safety at a cutoff depth instead of playing every line to checkmate.
scenario: A chess program cannot search to the end, so it scores material at a cutoff depth. What provides that score?
scenarioWrongs: A fully solved terminal value only
scenarioWhy: An evaluation function estimates a nonterminal position when the search must stop early.

definition: The encoding of facts and relationships in a form a program can store and reason with.
wrongs: The hardware sensors that collect raw percepts.
The expansion order of an uninformed search.
The random split of examples into a test set.
why: A representation such as logic or a semantic network makes knowledge available to an inference procedure.
example: A campus advisor encodes 'CEIT-6004 requires the introductory programming course' as a sentence in a knowledge base.
scenario: An advisor program must store course rules so it can draw conclusions later. Which AI task is the storing of those rules?
scenarioWhy: Knowledge representation is the encoding of the rules in a form the program can reason over.

definition: A stored set of sentences about a domain that an inference procedure can query and extend.
wrongs: The list of nodes waiting on a search frontier.
A table of unlabeled pictures with no stated facts.
The motors of a robot.
why: The knowledge base holds the axioms and derived facts that inference uses.
example: A medical tutor stores sentences about symptoms and illnesses and adds a new fact when a rule fires.
scenario: A tutor program keeps domain sentences and adds a new fact when a rule applies. Where are those sentences kept?
scenarioWhy: A knowledge base is the store of sentences that inference reads and extends.

definition: The process of deriving new sentences that follow from the sentences already in a knowledge base.
wrongs: The process of sensing the world through a camera.
The process of expanding the shallowest search node.
The process of fitting weights only to minimize training error.
why: Inference applies rules of entailment so a conclusion is supported by what is already stored.
example: From 'all lab sections meet on Friday' and 'section B is a lab,' the program derives that section B meets on Friday.
scenario: A program concludes that section B meets on Friday because of two stored sentences. What process produced that conclusion?
scenarioWhy: Inference derives the new sentence from sentences already in the knowledge base.

definition: Inference that starts from known facts and applies rules to derive new facts until a goal appears or no rule fires.
wrongs: Inference that starts from a hypothesis and looks backward for supporting facts.
A search from the goal state back to the start on a map.
Learning that adjusts a model from labeled pairs.
why: Forward chaining is data-driven: each new fact may trigger further rules.
example: A diagnostic system starts from observed symptoms and fires rules until it derives a likely fault.
scenario: A diagnostic program starts from observed symptoms and fires rules to reach a fault. Which inference direction is that?
scenarioWhy: Forward chaining begins with the known symptoms and works forward through the rules.

definition: Inference that starts from a goal and looks for rules and facts that would support it.
wrongs: Inference that starts from data and fires every matching rule forward.
A breadth-first search that ignores logic rules.
A local search that climbs an objective function.
why: Backward chaining is goal-driven and only explores rules relevant to the current goal.
example: To prove a student can graduate, an advisor program looks backward for the required courses on the transcript.
scenario: An advisor starts from the goal 'can graduate' and searches for rules and transcript facts that support it. Which method is that?
scenarioWhy: Backward chaining starts at the goal and looks for support, rather than firing every data rule.

definition: A program that answers problems in a narrow domain by applying a knowledge base through an inference engine.
wrongs: A general web search engine with no encoded domain rules.
A sort procedure for integers.
A robot motor controller with no stored expertise.
why: The classic split is a knowledge base of expert rules plus an inference engine that applies them.
example: A plant-diagnosis program uses expert if-then rules about leaves and soil to suggest a likely cause.
scenario: A narrow program uses expert if-then rules and an inference engine to suggest why a plant is wilting. What kind of program is it?
scenarioWrongs: A motor controller with no rules
scenarioWhy: An expert system applies a domain knowledge base through an inference engine.

definition: A representation of concepts as nodes and of relations between them as labeled edges.
wrongs: A table of numbers used only to train a classifier.
A queue of search nodes ordered by path cost.
A list of actuator voltages.
why: The graph makes inheritance and relationships explicit, such as an edge meaning 'is a kind of.'
example: A diagram links 'sparrow' to 'bird' with an is-a edge and 'bird' to 'can fly' with a property edge.
scenario: Course concepts are drawn as nodes, with edges such as 'is a kind of' between them. Which representation is that?
scenarioWhy: A semantic network represents concepts as nodes and their relations as labeled links.

definition: An explicit specification of the concepts, properties, and relations in a domain.
wrongs: A single numeric heuristic for a map.
The random initial state of a local search.
A performance score for one agent run.
why: An ontology fixes what kinds of things exist in the domain and how they may be related.
example: A university ontology defines Student, Course, and Instructor and the relation 'teaches' between Instructor and Course.
scenario: Modelers formally list the types Student and Course and the relation 'enrolled in' before writing rules. What are they writing?
scenarioWhy: An ontology specifies the domain's concepts and the relations allowed among them.

definition: The AI subfield in which a program improves its performance on a task from data or experience.
wrongs: The subfield that only hand-writes every decision rule and never uses data.
The study of sorting and shortest paths with no learning.
The design of logic gates in a processor.
why: Machine learning is one part of AI, focused on improvement from examples or experience rather than only hand-coded rules.
example: A spam filter improves after it is shown many messages already marked spam or not spam.
scenario: Instead of writing every spam rule by hand, a program improves from messages already marked spam or not. Which subfield is that?
scenarioWrongs: Manual rule writing with no data
scenarioWhy: Machine learning is the subfield in which performance improves from data or experience.

definition: Learning a mapping from inputs to outputs by using examples that already include the correct output label.
wrongs: Learning structure from inputs that have no output labels.
Learning only by rewards received after a sequence of actions, with no correct label per step.
Solving a maze by breadth-first search with no examples.
why: The training pairs supply the target output, so the learner can measure mistakes against that label.
example: A program learns to predict exam pass or fail from study hours, using past students whose outcomes are already known.
scenario: Past students have recorded study hours and a known pass or fail result, and a model learns from those pairs. Which learning setting is that?
scenarioWrongs: Clustering with no pass or fail labels
scenarioWhy: Supervised learning uses examples that already contain the correct output label.

definition: Learning structure or groupings from inputs that are not accompanied by output labels.
wrongs: Learning from examples that each include the correct class label.
Proving a goal from a knowledge base of logical sentences.
Expanding a game tree with minimax.
why: Without labels, the learner looks for patterns such as clusters in the inputs themselves.
example: A program groups shoppers by purchase records without being told any group name in advance.
scenario: Purchase records have no category labels, and a program groups similar shoppers anyway. Which learning setting is that?
scenarioWhy: Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabeled inputs.

definition: A fit that matches the training examples too closely, including their noise, and then performs poorly on new examples.
wrongs: A model too simple to capture the pattern, with high error even on the training examples.
A search that is optimal on every map.
A heuristic that is admissible for every state.
why: Overfitting memorizes peculiarities of the training set that do not repeat in unseen data.
example: A curve twists to touch every training point, including one mistyped grade, and then misses new students badly.
scenario: A model passes through every training point, including an obvious typo, and then misses new students. What has happened?
scenarioWhy: Overfitting matches training noise, such as the typo, and therefore fails to generalize.

definition: The collection of examples used to build or fit a model before it is judged on unseen data.
wrongs: The held-out examples used only for a final check and not for fitting.
The frontier of nodes in a graph search.
The rule list of an expert system written entirely by hand.
why: The learner adjusts the model on the training set, so that set must be kept distinct from a later test.
example: A classifier is fit on 800 labeled emails and later scored on 200 emails it did not use for fitting.
scenario: A student fits a classifier on 800 labeled emails and saves 200 others for a later score. What are the 800 emails?
scenarioWhy: The training set is the collection of examples used to fit the model.

definition: How well a model performs on new examples that were not used to fit it.
wrongs: How closely a model reproduces only the training rows, including their typos.
How fast breadth-first search expands the first level.
How many rules an expert types by hand.
why: Generalization is the point of learning: success on unseen cases, not a perfect recitation of the training set.
example: After fitting on last year's emails, a spam filter correctly labels a new email that arrived this morning.
scenario: A spam filter was fit on last year's mail and correctly labels a message that arrived today. What ability is it showing?
scenarioWhy: Generalization is successful performance on a new example that was not part of fitting.
